claim: The V1 rehearsal ran end to end as an outside user: a worker who followed only the public documentation put the GitHub Action on a repository we do not control, against a real task, and got a PR comment with six evidenced findings in 8m52s. The five 2.4.7 findings sit far inside the rule's own margin — holds of 1, 5 and 24ms against a 633ms floor for real focus transitions, and two orphaned focusouts needing no threshold at all. The individual-log read that rules.ts:699 requires for any real-page 2.4.7 finding has NOT been done, by worker-audit or by me, and the record says so rather than counting six as confirmed.
boardClaim: Someone following only our public instructions pointed the tool at a site we do not own and got six specific, evidenced findings in under nine minutes.
evidence: A worker acting as an outside user set the tool up from the published instructions alone, pointed it at a large public code-hosting page we do not control, and gave it a real task — find the repository's licence. It ran in under nine minutes and returned a comment naming six specific problems a screen-reader user would meet, each quoting what the screen reader actually said. Five of the six are the same kind of fault: a control takes keyboard focus and script removes it again in a thousandth to a fortieth of a second, too fast for anyone to see where they are. That number is not close to a judgement call — the fastest ordinary focus movement this project has ever measured is six hundred and thirty-three thousandths of a second, twenty-five times slower. Two of the five are a sharper case still, where focus was taken away before the browser had finished giving it. What this does NOT yet claim: the project's own rule requires each such finding on a real page to be read individually against its stored record before it is treated as settled, and that has not been done. Three of the six describe the same control, so six findings are four distinct controls. And the underlying measurement is known not to be perfectly repeatable, so this is what one run found rather than what the page contains. The run also took 8m52s against published guidance of five to eight minutes — one sample on a different shape of page, noted rather than treated as a correction.
